summary: This standards-track RFC provides the External Data Representation (XDR) description of NFS version 4 minor version 2, the machine-readable definition of its data structures.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 7863 is the code-level description of the NFS 4.2 file-sharing protocol. It lists every data structure, constant and error code, in a notation that a program can be generated from. The RFC even gives a short script that pulls the description out of the document, so implementers do not have to retype it.

subtitle: The machine-readable blueprint of the NFS version 4.2 protocol: every structure, constant and error code on the wire.

tldr.problem: An NFS version 4.2 implementation needs an exact definition of every structure it puts on the wire, and that definition is too long to live inside the protocol document.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC carries the External Data Representation description of NFSv4.2 as a block of lines marked with a sentinel, so a short shell script can extract it from the document into a file that compiles directly.
tldr.outcome: Implementers get one authoritative file that defines the encoding of NFSv4.2 messages, while the protocol document keeps to the rules and the reason. The security and IANA sections simply point at the protocol RFC.

today: RFC 7863 is a Proposed Standard and has not been obsoleted. It remains the machine-readable XDR description of the NFS version 4.2 protocol described in RFC 7862, and it points readers to that document for the security and IANA considerations.

sections.title: What This Document Contains
sections.content:
This document provides the External Data Representation (XDR) description of the NFS version 4 minor version 2 protocol, which is specified in RFC 7862. XDR is defined in RFC 4506. In short, the RFC is the wire format of NFSv4.2 written out in a notation that describes types rather than bytes: structures, unions, enumerations, arrays and the fixed-size types they are built from.

So that implementations which support all of NFSv4.0, NFSv4.1 and NFSv4.2 can share one description, the text includes operations and features of NFSv4.0 and NFSv4.1 that do not apply to NFSv4.2. It is fully compatible with the specification for NFSv4.0 in RFC 7531, with one exception: the clientaddr4 structure has been replaced by, strictly aliased to, netaddr4, which has the same members with the same purposes under different names, r_netid becoming na_r_netid and r_addr becoming na_addr. This effectively reconverges the NFSv4.0 and NFSv4.1 strands of the XDR into one.

The description itself is the whole of Section 2 of the RFC. Sections 3 and 4 point at the security considerations and the IANA considerations of RFC 7862 instead of repeating them.
sections.plainLanguage: NFS 4.2 is a protocol for sharing files over a network, and the rules for how it is written on the wire are too long to sit in the protocol document itself. This RFC is that reference, written in a type notation rather than in prose. It also keeps the older NFS 4.0 and 4.1 material inside the same file, so one description serves implementations that support all three versions.

sections.title: Getting the Machine-Readable Description
sections.content:
The XDR description is written so that it can be extracted into a form that is ready to compile. The RFC gives a shell script that does the extraction:

#!/bin/sh
grep "^  *///" | sed 's?^  */// ??' | sed 's?^  *///$??'

With that script stored in a file called extract.sh and the RFC itself in a file called spec.txt, the reader runs sh extract.sh < spec.txt > nfs4_prot.x. The script removes the leading white space from each line, plus the sentinel sequence of three slashes, so the result is the XDR description on its own.

The extracted file begins with a notice that it was machine generated for RFC 7862, carries the IETF Trust copyright and licence terms, and defines the NFS version 4.2 program interface.
sections.plainLanguage: Every line of the description starts with three slashes, which marks it as part of the extractable block. The script finds those lines, strips the marker and the indentation, and writes what is left to a file that a compiler can take. The result is a single file holding the whole NFSv4.2 interface.

sections.title: Constants, File Types and Status Codes
sections.content:
The description opens with the fixed sizes the protocol uses: a file handle is 128 octets, a verifier is 8 octets, the 'other' field is 12 octets, opaque data is limited to 1024 octets and a session identifier is 16 octets. The 64-bit and 32-bit maximum values are given alongside them, and the maximum file length and file offset are both close to the full 64-bit range.

A file type enumeration gives nine values, from 1 for a regular file through 2 for a directory, 3 for a block device, 4 for a character device, 5 for a symbolic link, 6 for a socket and 7 for a fifo, to 8 for an attribute directory and 9 for a named attribute.

The status enumeration is the error list the server returns. It mixes small numbers inherited from NFS version 3 with a block of larger values reserved for NFS version 4. The low numbers are familiar ones such as permission denied, no such file, hard I/O error, access denied, file already exists and different file systems. The version 4 values start at 10001 with an illegal file handle, and run through codes for a stale read directory cookie, an unsupported operation, a response limit exceeded, an undefined server error, a lock that is unavailable or expired, a grace period, a wrong security flavour, a minor version mismatch, and a set of codes above 10040 that belong to NFS version 4.2, including offload and copy failures.
sections.plainLanguage: The description fixes the sizes of everything that has a fixed size, such as the file handle and the session identifier, and it lists the file types a server can report. The largest part is the status list, which is the protocol's error table: a small set of numbers inherited from NFS version 3 and a much larger set reserved for version 4, including the new codes that version 4.2 added for its copy and offload operations.

sections.title: The COMPOUND Procedure and the Operation Unions
sections.content:
Everything a client sends travels in one remote procedure call. The COMPOUND4args structure holds a tag string, a minor version number and an array of arguments, and the matching COMPOUND4res structure holds a status, the same tag and an array of results. The argument array is a union switched on the operation number, and the result array is a second union switched on the same numbers, so each operation contributes one arm to each union.

Most operation results are themselves unions switched on the status code, so the status says which arm carries meaning. A union that switches on nfsstat4 has an arm for NFS4_OK and a default arm, and several of them use void for the default arm so that nothing is sent when the operation failed.

The program definition ties this together. The NFS program number is 100003, its version is 4, and it has two procedures: a null procedure at 0 and the compound procedure at 1. The description also defines the callback channel the server uses to call back into the client, as a separate program in the transient range, with the client passing the exact number to the server through the create session or backchannel control operations.
sections.plainLanguage: A client sends one call that holds a list of operations, and the server answers with a matching list of results. Each operation number selects one arm of a union on the way out and one on the way back, and each result carries a status that says whether it succeeded. The whole thing is a single remote procedure call on program number 100003, version 4.

sections.title: The Operations New in NFSv4.2
sections.content:
The operation enumeration separates the operations by the version that introduced them. The base set runs from 3 for access to 39 for releasing a lock owner, and includes several marked as mandatory not to implement. The NFSv4.1 set adds operations numbered 40 to 58, among them the backchannel control, exchange identifier, create session and destroy session operations, and the layout operations used for data placement. The NFSv4.2 set adds thirteen more, numbered 59 to 71.

The new operations are allocate, copy, copy notify, deallocate, IO advise, layout error, layout stats, offload cancel, offload status, read plus, seek, write same and clone. Their argument structures show what each one needs. Copy takes a source and a destination state identifier, source and destination offsets, a count, flags saying whether the copy must be consecutive and whether it is synchronous, and a list of source servers. Write same takes a state identifier, a stability setting and an application data block. Seek takes a state identifier, an offset and a description of what to seek to, and its result carries a flag for end of file and the resulting offset.
sections.plainLanguage: NFS 4.2 added thirteen operations on top of the earlier ones. They cover moving data: allocating space, copying a range between two files, deallocating it, writing the same block at many offsets, seeking to a position, reading with a hint, and cloning a file. The copy operation also carries the list of servers that hold the source data, so the copy can be spread across them.

sections.title: Security and IANA Considerations
sections.content:
The RFC adds no security considerations of its own. Its Section 3 points readers to the security considerations section of RFC 7862, and its Section 4 does the same for the IANA considerations. That is consistent with the role of the document: it describes the encoding, and the security rules live with the protocol they belong to.

The normative references are the requirements language document, the XDR standard, the NFS version 4.1 XDR description, the NFS version 4 XDR description, and the NFS version 4.2 protocol document itself.
sections.plainLanguage: This RFC says nothing about security itself. It points at the protocol RFC, where the security rules are stated, and at the same place for the registry entries. The reason is simple: this document only describes the format of the messages, and the rules about protecting them belong with the protocol.
